headline: High risk of shared-repo write conflicts and medium risk of prompt/data leakage when Aider and AutoGen are paired in default code-execution setups.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Aider reads and edits repo files, and AutoGen can pass application data into agents; if AutoGen forwards Aider-authored file content into prompts, injected instructions can propagate. The pair lacks any documented provenance or isolation mechanism, so the pathway is plausible in default shared-workspace use, though not as direct as a raw web-content bridge.
conditions: IF AutoGen includes Aider-edited file contents in agent prompts without provenance filtering, injection risk materializes.
IF both agents operate on the same repository or working directory, malicious instructions in files can bridge them.
mitigations: Separate the agents into distinct working directories.
Strip or sandbox untrusted file content before prompting AutoGen.
Require explicit human review for any instruction-like text in repo files.
Use a provenance tag or allowlist for prompt sources.
requires-engineering: add parser-level instruction/content separation.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Aider touches source code and git history, while AutoGen handles application data and can use broad network egress through configured model providers. In a shared workspace, sensitive code or secrets can flow from Aider into AutoGen prompts and then out to third-party APIs. This is a default-path concern unless the operator isolates data flows.
conditions: IF both agents can read the same repository or workspace, code and history may be exposed to AutoGen.
IF AutoGen forwards prompt context to external model providers, shared sensitive content can leave the local environment.
mitigations: Use separate repos or cloned worktrees per agent.
Redact secrets before handing files to AutoGen.
Disable external model calls for sensitive tasks.
Limit AutoGen inputs to minimal excerpts.
requires-engineering: enforce data-loss-prevention filters on agent handoff.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Aider can write the filesystem and modify git state, and AutoGen can also write the filesystem and execute code in local or Docker executors. Both therefore have overlapping write authority over the same repo, and Aider explicitly shares state via a shared git repo. Without locking, concurrent edits and git mutations can corrupt work or overwrite each other.
conditions: IF both agents target the same git repository, concurrent writes can conflict.
IF AutoGen uses a local executor against the same directory, it can race with Aider's git commits.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate branch.
Pause one agent while the other writes.
Use file locks around shared paths.
Review and merge commits manually after each turn.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Aider produces code edits and git commits, and AutoGen is a multi-agent framework that can act on agent outputs through tool calls and code execution. If AutoGen treats Aider's output as authoritative, mistakes can cascade into further edits or actions. The pair is not inherently self-verifying, so the risk exists in default orchestration patterns.
conditions: IF AutoGen consumes Aider's generated patches or summaries without verification, errors can propagate.
IF downstream AutoGen agents are allowed to execute code based on Aider output, the cascade widens.
mitigations: Require a verification step before acting on Aider output.
Compare generated diffs against tests or lint results.
Restrict AutoGen to read-only review mode for Aider outputs.
Escalate ambiguous changes to a human reviewer.
requires-engineering: add automated output validation gates.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and touch code or application data, but neither profile states regulated-data handling, residency, or retention mismatches. The only concrete compliance concern is that Aider handles model provider API keys and AutoGen sends calls to configured model providers, which can matter if sensitive code is routed externally. The evidence is insufficient for a stronger finding.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into prompts sent to external model providers, compliance obligations may be triggered.
IF the operator requires on-prem-only processing, external API calls violate that policy.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of prompts.
Use approved enterprise model endpoints only.
Review retention terms for configured providers.
Document data-flow boundaries for the pair.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for residency and retention.
